label: thm:well-posed
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:well-posed}
    For a smooth and connected domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, with $d\geq1$, let $V$ be a closed subspace of the Sobolev space $W^{1,r}(\Omega)$ with $r > 1$. Assume that the energy functional $\mathcal{F}:V\to\mathbb{R}$ is convex and coercive in the following sense: for any sequence $\boldsymbol{u}_n$ in $V$ such that $\|\boldsymbol{u}_n\|_V \to \infty$, it follows that $\mathcal{F}(\boldsymbol{u}_n)\to\infty$. Then there exists a minimizer of $\mathcal{F}$ in $V$. Moreover, if $\mathcal{F}$ is strictly convex, this minimizer is unique.

label: remark:extension-well-posedness
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark:extension-well-posedness}
A possible avenue for extending the validity of \cref{thm:well-posed} to $r=1$ could involve the space of vector fields of bounded deformation in $\Omega$, denoted by $BD(\Omega)$ \cite{temam1985}. This space consists of the set of vector fields in $L^1(\Omega)$ whose symmetric gradients belong to the space of matrix-valued Radon measures. By relaxing the definition of the energy functional to incorporate measure-valued derivatives, one can show that, under linear growth conditions, the energy functional is coercive and, via a compactness argument, prove the existence of a minimizer. This extension will be explored in future work.

label: thm:properties_j
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:properties_j}
Let the constitutive law be defined in terms of a differentiable local dissipation potential $j=j(\alpha,\beta)$ via \eqref{eq:viscous_stresses_j}. Assume that the following properties hold: 1) $j$ is convex, 2) $j$ is increasing in $\beta$, and 3) the gradient $\nabla_{\iota}j := (\frac{\partial j}{\partial \alpha}, \frac{\partial j}{\partial \beta})^\top$ is zero when $(\alpha,\beta) = (0,0)$. Then, the constitutive law is frame-indifferent, dissipative, and is derived from the convex dissipation potential $\mathcal{J}$ defined in \eqref{eq:dissipation_potential}.

title: Results
body_md: The optimal loss values and relative $L^2$ velocity errors for the test problem over all architectures and initializations are shown in \cref{tab:ns_test_error}. The best results are obtained with the ICNNE model with network (20). This model is used to compute the velocity fields shown in the top row of \cref{fig:ns_results}, whose right panel compares the learned potential with the exact potential and the initial guess. The bottom row of this figure shows the decay of the loss over the L-BFGS function evaluations and the learned effective shear and bulk viscosities along $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=0$, respectively. In \cref{tab:ns_test_error}, for the ICNN and SNN models, we observe that, despite the training being stalled due to Newton's method failing, the models are still capable of solving the test problem successfully, although a very large relative error is achieved in these cases.

title: Results
body_md: The optimal loss values and relative $L^2$ velocity errors for the extrusion test problem are shown in \cref{tab:hb_test_error}. The best results are obtained with the ICNNE model with network (5 5); the right panel of \cref{fig:hb_results} shows the dissipation potential of this model. Although the method of \cite{sunol2025} achieves the same loss value during training as our best ICNNE model, it produces a larger test error than the ICNNE model. Similarly to the NS problem, we observe in \cref{tab:hb_test_error} that, for the SNNE and SNNsq models, the best test error is achieved by a model that fails to complete the PDE-based training, yet successfully solves the test problem. In the case of the SNNE and SNNsq models, the LBFGS method during training broke down early on, such that the final fluid model is very close to the Newtonian model used in the initialization. This explains the very low number of iterations required for solving the test problems for SNNE and SNNsq in table \ref{tab:hb_test_error}.

title: Results
body_md: The optimal loss values and relative $L^2$ velocity errors for the test problem are presented in \cref{tab:vp_test}. In \cref{fig:vp_results}, we also plot results and the dissipation potential of the model that achieves the lowest test error, an ICNNE model with a (5 5) architecture. The test case we consider is particularly challenging due to the strong discontinuities in the concentration field (see \cref{fig:vp_setup}). As a result, Newton's method is incapable of converging for practically all non-ICNNE models. The ICNNE model achieves an optimal test error which is almost one order of magnitude lower than the other models, and only one in four ICNNE models fail to converge when solving the test problem. The middle panel in \cref{fig:vp_results} shows that the learned dissipation potential closely matches the exact potential over the range of strain rates present in the training data.

title: Results
body_md: In \cref{tab:subzero_comparison}, we present the optimal values of the loss function $\mathcal{L}(\theta)$; the best fit is achieved with the ICNNE (10 10) architecture. The potential computed with this model is plotted in the right panel of \cref{fig:subzero_results}; interestingly, the potential presents much larger values for $\alpha < 0$, indicating resistance to shear is much larger under compressive rather than expansive strain-rates, something to be expected in a DEM where particles do not stick. In the middle panels of \cref{fig:subzero_results}, we compare the velocities computed with this model with the data.
